I definitely agree that this sort of "brute-force" approach isn't elegant or particularly appealing. As far as it being a lot of work, to me that's just the name of the game. Whilst there are major performance improvements that can come with relatively small changes, such as your libcpp change, there's only so many of those. At some point, if we want to squeeze out all the performance we can, we are going to need to do the tedious changes. 
If we push this idea to all files though, it actually becomes easier, as a simple python script could do it. That would be one noisy PR though. Find all files that use `ClassDB`, add it in their includes, and remove it everywhere else.

Currently, as per my measuring tool, `ClassDB` is in ~3000 compile units. Getting it down to ~900 would already be a 70% reduction in overhead. Looking at the tracker's measurement, that would reduce it from 600s on fresh compile and 660s on recompile to around 180s and 200s relatively. 
Also, this work is reducing the overhead on `ref_counted.h` and `resource.h` which are also some of our most expensive compile-wise. 

To some extent, moving closer to google's standard of Include What You Use, and thus only what you use, will be beneficial both for compile cost and for code clarity. This would be helpful long-term for development efforts, as any person modifying/replacing any existing framework, such as `ClassDB` as is currently underway, would only need to look up `#include "core/object/class_db.h"` and would be able to find exactly where it is being used and how, and make sure their new solution works. It would also reduce the number of times you need to re-compile to find every single compile unit that is no longer happy, since they would all be explicit about what they require to compile. This feels like a bigger discussion than this excessive-compilation-time-related work and PR, so I think I should open a discussion/issue regarding that or maybe discuss it on Rocket Chat first. What's your opinion?

> If we push this idea to all files though, it actually becomes easier, as a simple python script could do it. That would be one noisy PR though. Find all files that use ClassDB, add it in their includes, and remove it everywhere else.

This is an interesting idea. Could be worthy of pursuit, though I suspect we'd still need a good amount of work on top of it.

> Currently, as per my measuring tool, ClassDB is in ~3000 compile units. Getting it down to ~900 would already be a 70% reduction in overhead.

Those are some good numbers, thanks! This is a much better ratio than I'd have guessed.

> To some extent, moving closer to google's standard of Include What You Use, and thus only what you use, will be beneficial both for compile cost and for code clarity. 
> This feels like a bigger discussion than this excessive-compilation-time-related work and PR, so I think I should open a discussion/issue regarding that or maybe discuss it on Rocket Chat first. What's your opinion?

I would also prefer a IWYU-style long term, but yea, this would need discussion. If we wanted to bring this into discussion, I think a godot implementation proposal would be most appropriate (assuming there isn't one already).

IWYU requires a lot of stricture to ensure they are removed correctly as well, or it will quickly lead to a lot of clutter as things change, even without IWYU we still have a lot of redundant includes and even unused includes due to various refactors and other changes that removed various uses of types, this is AFAIK one of the reasons we don't use IWYU

IWYU automatically removes includes that are unused, so this should (overall) remove the total number of deep includes across our codebase. But it does have downsides / bugs, maintenance cost, and is not a silver bullet, so I'm also not sure how feasible integrating it into CI really is.

Not everyone has IWYU integrated and unless it's available for CI we shouldn't requite it for contributors

But it would be less clutter if we exclude a large number of basic includes and root types, standard includes like `object.h`, `ref_counter.h`, `resource.h`, math stuff, container and variant stuff, as well as error includes and `typedefs.h`

It would also have to be used correctly with respect to forward declares and be trivial to configure for that or it will do a lot more harm in a lot of cases, we already have issues with inexperienced contributors not using forward declarations enough and that's without them potentially fighting IWYU as well

Beyond the ideas of an IWYU-style codebase, I think this PR (and `ref_counted.h` one) should still be included, as they work towards removing unnecessary includes. 
As shown by the 70% reduction potential, I think it's worth it. 

Looking at the remaining heavy hitters, it looks like theres only a dozen or so left to fix to get rid of the issue. Might seem like a lot but it really isn't that bad. 
Funny enough, `image.h`, `input.h`, `input_event.h`, and all the headers in scene/ which I added it to through this PR are big culprits even though I didn't think so when I did. 

Q: Should I remove it from there as part of this PR, to try and get the number to be lower? These are cascading changes from this change after all.
